Yibo data/Q2/explanation.txt: In 2021, Victoria recorded the highest number of hospitalised road traffic injuries (11,130), followed by Queensland (10,447) and New South Wales (9,003). Together, these three jurisdictions accounted for approximately 77.4% of the national count. The territories recorded substantially lower counts, with the Northern Territory reporting 710 and the Australian Capital Territory 740. These figures are absolute counts rather than population-standardised rates. Therefore, lower counts in smaller jurisdictions do not necessarily indicate lower individual risk.
Yibo data/Q3/explanation.txt: In 2021, people aged 40–64 recorded the largest number of hospitalised road traffic injuries (13,026), followed by those aged 26–39 (9,423) and 17–25 (8,010). Together, these three groups accounted for approximately 77.1% of all hospitalisations. The age bands have unequal widths; for example, 40–64 covers 25 years while 65–74 covers 10 years. These absolute counts therefore do not show an individual’s age-specific risk.
Yibo data/Q4/explanation.txt: Male hospitalisations remained substantially higher than female hospitalisations throughout 2011–2021. Male cases increased from 22,321 in 2011 to 25,788 in 2021, while female cases increased from 11,712 to 13,716. Males consistently accounted for approximately two-thirds of hospitalisations. The 2020 decline was much larger among females: female hospitalisations fell from 14,499 in 2019 to 12,781 in 2020, while the male count declined only slightly from 25,365 to 25,178. These are counts, not sex-specific population rates or exposure-adjusted risks.
Yibo data/Q5/explanation.txt: Vehicle occupants recorded the largest number of hospitalisations in 2021 (19,524), representing approximately 49.4% of the national total. Motorcyclists accounted for 8,883 cases (22.5%) and cyclists for 8,163 (20.7%). Pedestrians recorded 2,334 cases (5.9%). These counts do not account for differences in travel frequency, distance travelled, or population exposure. They therefore describe the composition of hospitalisations, not the risk per trip or kilometre.
Yibo data/E1/explanation.txt: The change was not uniform across road users. Cyclists increased from 15.8% of hospitalisations in 2011 to 21.9% in 2020. Although the share fell slightly to 20.7% in 2021, it remained above both 2019 (18.3%) and 2011. Vehicle occupants fell from approximately 52.0% to 49.4%, while motorcyclists remained relatively stable at around 22%–23%. The 2020 disruption therefore coincided with a lasting elevation in the cyclist share.
Yibo data/E2/explanation.txt: Between 2011 and 2021, growth among older adults was concentrated among car drivers and pedal cyclists rather than pedestrians. Among people aged 40–64, cyclist hospitalisations increased by 1,376 and car-driver hospitalisations by 564, whereas pedestrian hospitalisations decreased by 11. Cyclist increases were also evident among ages 65–74 (+509) and 75+ (+198). In contrast, pedestrian changes among older groups were small or negative: +8 for ages 65–74 and −77 for ages 75+. The findings indicate that the increase among older adults was primarily associated with cycling and driving, rather than pedestrian injuries. The largest decline occurred among pedestrians aged 17–25 (−194), while car-driver hospitalisations increased most among ages 26–39 (+781). These are changes in absolute counts. Population ageing and changes in travel exposure are not controlled for, so the results do not demonstrate changes in individual risk.
Yibo data/E3/E3a/explanation.txt: The groups contributing the most hospitalisations did not always contribute the same share of bed days. Cyclists accounted for 19.02% of hospitalisations but only 11.13% of bed days. In contrast, pedestrians accounted for only 6.49% of hospitalisations but 13.14% of bed days. Motorcyclists also had a higher bed-day share (25.02%) than hospitalisation share (22.27%). Road-user results showed a similar mismatch. Pedestrians accounted for 6.49% of hospitalisations but 13.14% of bed days, whereas cyclists accounted for 19.02% of hospitalisations but only 11.13% of bed days. Therefore, groups with the most hospitalisations were not necessarily those generating the greatest hospital burden.
Yibo data/E3/E3b/explanation.txt: From 2016 to 2021, people aged 40–64 accounted for the largest shares of both hospitalisations (32.82%) and bed days (34.17%). However, older age groups showed a disproportionate bed-day burden. People aged 75 and over represented only 6.23% of hospitalisations but 13.29% of bed days, while those aged 65–74 accounted for 7.31% of hospitalisations but 11.18% of bed days. In contrast, people aged 8–16 represented 6.61% of hospitalisations but only 3.53% of bed days. These results suggest that hospitalisations among older adults tend to consume more hospital resources relative to their case numbers. Bed days indicate healthcare resource use, but they should not be interpreted as a complete measure of injury severity because length of stay may also be affected by treatment needs, comorbidities, discharge arrangements, and other factors.
